title: Olympiad angle chasing
blurb: Cyclic quadrilaterals, directed angles and the standard configurations, used to write complete synthetic proofs.
outcomes: Prove and use the converses of the cyclic and tangent criteria
Run an angle chase with directed angles that works in every configuration
Recognise orthocentre, antiparallel and incentre-excentre configurations and write BMO-standard proofs
lesson:
Here is a fact worth owning. In an acute triangle $ABC$ with orthocentre $H$, the reflection of $H$ in $BC$ lies on the circumcircle. Let $BE$ and $CF$ be altitudes. The right angles at $E$ and $F$ put $A,F,H,E$ on a circle (the circle with diameter $AH$), so $\angle BHC=\angle FHE=180^\circ-\angle A$. The reflection $H'$ satisfies $\angle BH'C=\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle A$ and lies on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$, so the opposite angles of $ABH'C$ add to $180^\circ$ and it is cyclic.

Nothing there was clever. We found right angles, turned them into a circle, read an angle off that circle, and turned the angle into another circle. That loop (angles give circles, circles give angles) is the engine of olympiad angle chasing. This unit is about running it reliably: knowing the converses, handling configurations without drawing six cases, recognising the standard pictures, and writing proofs a marker cannot fault.

The toolkit, with converses

Cyclic criteria. Four points $A,B,C,D$, no three collinear, are concyclic if and only if either of the following holds: $\angle ABD=\angle ACD$ with $B,C$ on the same side of $AD$; or $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ with $B,D$ on opposite sides of $AC$.

Tangent criterion. A line $t$ through $A$ touches circle $ABC$ if and only if the angle between $t$ and chord $AB$ equals $\angle ACB$, the angle in the alternate segment.

Right angles. $\angle APB=90^\circ$ if and only if $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$.

The forward directions are the inscribed angle theorem. The converses are what make the method work, and they rest on one observation. Fix the segment $AD$ and a circle $\Gamma$ through $A$ and $D$. If $P$ is inside $\Gamma$ (on a given side of $AD$), extend $AP$ to meet the arc at $P'$; then $\angle APD$ is an exterior angle of triangle $PP'D$, so $\angle APD>\angle AP'D$. A point outside sees $AD$ at a smaller angle in the same way. So on one side of $AD$, the points seeing $AD$ at the angle given by the arc are exactly the points of that arc.

Directed angles

The weakness of these criteria is the side conditions. In a real problem a point may sit on a segment or beyond it, and the chase that says $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ in one picture says $\angle ABC=\angle ADC$ in another. The cure is to measure angles between lines, modulo $180^\circ$.

Directed angles. For lines $\ell,m$, let $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ be the angle through which $\ell$ must be turned anticlockwise to become parallel to $m$, taken modulo $180^\circ$, and write $\measuredangle ABC=\measuredangle(BA,BC)$. Then $\measuredangle(\ell,m)=-\measuredangle(m,\ell)$; $\measuredangle(\ell,m)+\measuredangle(m,n)=\measuredangle(\ell,n)$; $A,B,C$ are collinear iff $\measuredangle ABC=0$; and $\measuredangle ABC+\measuredangle BCA+\measuredangle CAB=0$ in every triangle.

Cyclic criterion: $A,B,C,D$ are concyclic iff $\measuredangle ABC=\measuredangle ADC$. Tangent criterion: $t$ touches circle $ABC$ at $A$ iff $\measuredangle(t,AB)=\measuredangle ACB$.

Why does the cyclic criterion cover both cases? If $B$ and $D$ are on the same side of $AC$, triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ have the same orientation, the directed angles are the ordinary ones with the same sign, and we recover equal angles. If they are on opposite sides, the orientations differ, say $\measuredangle ABC=\angle ABC$ and $\measuredangle ADC=-\angle ADC$, and equality modulo $180^\circ$ means $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$. One statement, both pictures.

Two warnings. First, you cannot halve: $2x=2y$ only gives $x=y$ or $x=y+90^\circ$, so central angles and angle bisectors need care. Route through a tangent instead. Second, directed angles forget which side of a line a point is on, so they cannot prove betweenness or compute "the angle is $40^\circ$". Use them for concyclicity, collinearity, parallels and tangency.

Configurations to know cold

The orthocentre. With feet $D,E,F$ of the altitudes, the quadrilaterals $AFHE$, $BDHF$, $CEHD$ (diameters $AH,BH,CH$) and $BCEF$, $CAFD$, $ABDE$ (diameters $BC,CA,AB$) are all cyclic. Also $\angle BAH=90^\circ-\angle B=\angle OAC$, so $AH$ and $AO$ are reflections of each other in the bisector of angle $A$.

Antiparallels. If $X$ on line $AB$ and $Y$ on line $AC$ make $B,C,Y,X$ concyclic, then $\measuredangle(XY,AB)=\measuredangle YXB=\measuredangle YCB=\measuredangle ACB$, which is the angle the tangent at $A$ makes with $AB$. So $XY$ is parallel to that tangent, hence perpendicular to $AO$.

Incentre-excentre lemma. Let line $AI$ meet the circumcircle again at $M$, where $I$ is the incentre and $I_A$ the $A$-excentre. Then $MB=MC=MI=MI_A$.

Proof: $M$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$, so $MB=MC$ and $\angle MBC=\angle MAC=\tfrac12\angle A$. Hence $\angle MBI=\tfrac12\angle A+\tfrac12\angle B$, and $\angle MIB$, an exterior angle of triangle $ABI$, is also $\tfrac12\angle A+\tfrac12\angle B$. So $MB=MI$. The internal and external bisectors at $B$ are perpendicular, so triangle $IBI_A$ has a right angle at $B$; the only point of the hypotenuse $II_A$ equidistant from $B$ and $I$ is its midpoint, so $M$ is that midpoint and $MI_A=MI$.

Worked examples

Example 1. Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcentre $O$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that $XY\perp AO$.

The first instinct is to compute lengths such as $AX=AD^2/AB$. It works, but it is messy and teaches nothing. Look for right angles instead: $\angle AXD=\angle AYD=90^\circ$, so $X$ and $Y$ lie on the circle with diameter $AD$, and that circle hands us an angle:

\[\angle AYX=\angle ADX=90^\circ-\angle DAB=\angle ABC.\]

So $B,C,Y,X$ are concyclic (exterior angle equals interior opposite angle), and by the antiparallel fact $XY\perp AO$. To finish by hand instead: triangle $AOC$ is isosceles with apex angle $2\angle B$, so $\angle OAC=90^\circ-\angle B$. If $AO$ meets $XY$ at $T$, triangle $ATY$ has angles $90^\circ-\angle B$ at $A$ and $\angle B$ at $Y$, leaving $90^\circ$ at $T$.

The habit to keep: two right angles on a common segment are a circle, and that circle moves an angle from one place to another.

Example 2. $BC$ is a fixed chord of a circle $\omega$, not a diameter, and $A$ moves on $\omega$. The circle through $A$ tangent to line $BC$ at $B$ meets line $AC$ again at $P$, and the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $C$ meets line $AB$ again at $Q$. Prove that lines $BP$ and $CQ$ pass through a fixed point.

Draw a few positions of $A$, on both arcs, and you will see $P$ jump from segment $AC$ to beyond $A$ or beyond $C$. An undirected chase would need cases. With directed angles there is one argument.

By the tangent criterion in circle $ABP$, $\measuredangle(BC,BP)=\measuredangle BAP=\measuredangle BAC$, the last step because $P$ lies on line $AC$. Now the key observation for any moving point: what stays constant? By the cyclic criterion, $\measuredangle BAC$ is the same for every point $A$ of $\omega$, whichever arc it is on. Call it $\theta$. So $BP$ is the line through $B$ at directed angle $\theta$ to $BC$: a fixed line. In the same way $\measuredangle(CB,CQ)=\measuredangle CAB=-\theta$, so $CQ$ is also a fixed line.

Two fixed lines meet at a fixed point unless they are parallel, which needs $2\theta=0$, that is $\angle BAC=90^\circ$ and $BC$ a diameter, which is excluded. We can even name the point. The tangent to $\omega$ at $B$ makes angle $\measuredangle(BC,t_B)=-\theta$, so line $BP$ is its mirror image in $BC$; likewise for $C$. Hence the fixed point is the reflection in $BC$ of the point $T$ where the tangents at $B$ and $C$ meet.

Example 3. Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB\neq AC$ and incentre $I$. The circle through $B$, $I$, $C$ meets line $AB$ again at $X$ and line $AC$ again at $Y$. Prove that $XY$ is tangent to the incircle.

Chasing gives $\angle AXY=\angle ACB$ quickly, since $B,C,Y,X$ are concyclic, but tangency is a statement about distance from $I$, and angles at $X$ and $Y$ will not deliver it. So ask what the configuration knows. By the incentre-excentre lemma, circle $BIC$ has centre $M$ on line $AI$. A circle centred on a line is symmetric in that line, and reflection in $AI$ swaps lines $AB$ and $AC$.

So the reflection $C^*$ of $C$ in $AI$ lies on the circle and on line $AB$, hence is $B$ or $X$. It is not $B$, because $AC^*=AC\neq AB$. Thus $X=C^*$ and similarly $Y=B^*$, so line $XY$ is the mirror image of line $BC$. The incircle is its own mirror image and touches $BC$, so it touches $XY$. As a bonus, $AX=AC$ and $AY=AB$.

When a circle's centre lies on an axis of symmetry of the figure, reflect.

Example 4. Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcentre $O$. The circle through $B$, $O$, $C$ meets lines $AB$ and $AC$ again at $D$ and $E$, different from $B$ and $C$. Prove that the reflection of $O$ in $DE$ lies on the circle through $A$, $D$, $E$.

The conclusion looks like the opening fact, so guess that $O$ is the orthocentre of $ADE$, and aim for $DO\perp AE$. Depending on the shape of $ABC$, $D$ may lie on segment $AB$ or beyond $B$, so we use directed angles.

The trap is $\measuredangle OCB$: the familiar $90^\circ-\angle A$ comes from halving $\angle BOC=2\angle A$, which is not allowed. Use the tangent $t$ at $C$ instead. Since $t\perp CO$, \[\measuredangle(CO,CB)=\measuredangle(CO,t)+\measuredangle(t,CB)=90^\circ+\measuredangle CAB.\] Now circle $BOCD$ and the line $ABD$ give \[\measuredangle(DO,AC)=\measuredangle ODB+\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle OCB+\measuredangle BAC=90^\circ+\measuredangle CAB+\measuredangle BAC=90^\circ.\]

So $DO\perp AE$, and swapping the roles of $B$ and $C$ gives $EO\perp AD$: $O$ is the orthocentre of $ADE$. (The triangle is genuine: $A$ cannot lie on circle $BOC$, as it sees $BC$ at $\angle A$, not $2\angle A$.) To finish without asking whether $ADE$ is acute, redo the opening fact with directed angles. Turning both lines through $90^\circ$ gives $\measuredangle DOE=\measuredangle(AE,AD)=\measuredangle EAD$. Reflection reverses directed angles, so the reflection $O'$ satisfies $\measuredangle DO'E=\measuredangle DAE$, and $A,D,E,O'$ are concyclic.

Writing it up

A BMO marker wants a proof that is correct in every configuration and checkable line by line. Say at the start if you use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. Give a reason for every equality (which circle, which collinearity, which tangent). Prove a concyclicity before you use it. Deal with degenerate cases in a sentence. A diagram is a guide, never a justification.

Common traps.

  • Proving the result only for your drawing when a point could lie on a segment or its extension.
  • Halving directed angles, for instance with central angles or bisectors.
  • Using "it looks cyclic" in place of a criterion.
  • Circular reasoning: when the claim is that $P$ lies on a circle, do not draw $P$ on it and read off angles. Prove an angle equality, or define $P'$ on the circle and show $P'=P$.
  • Trying to get betweenness or an actual angle size out of directed angles.

How to spot this in a contest

Reach for these tools when the conclusion is concyclicity, collinearity, parallel or perpendicular lines, or tangency, and the data are angles, right angles, tangents or circles. Mark every right angle and every tangent first: each is a circle or an angle equality waiting to be used. If you see an orthocentre, an incentre, an arc midpoint or a circumcentre, recall the standard facts before chasing blindly. If the chase stalls, draw an accurate figure and look for four points that seem concyclic but have not been joined yet; prove that as a lemma. And if a point moves, ask which directed angle stays fixed.

practice.q: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle BAC=58^\circ$ and $\angle ABC=80^\circ$. Let $O$ be its circumcentre and $H$ its orthocentre. Find $\angle OAH$.
practice.hint: Work out $\angle BAH$ and $\angle OAC$ separately in terms of the angles of the triangle.
practice.sol:
The triangle has $\angle C=42^\circ$, so it is acute and both $O$ and $H$ lie inside it. Since $AH\perp BC$, the right-angled triangle $ABD$ (with $D$ the foot of the altitude) gives $\angle BAH=90^\circ-\angle B=10^\circ$. Triangle $AOC$ is isosceles with $\angle AOC=2\angle B=160^\circ$, so $\angle OAC=10^\circ$ as well.

The rays $AH$ and $AO$ therefore make $10^\circ$ with $AB$ and with $AC$ respectively, and since $10^\circ+10^\circ<58^\circ$ they lie in that order inside angle $BAC$. Hence $\angle OAH=58^\circ-10^\circ-10^\circ=38^\circ$. In general $\angle OAH=|\angle B-\angle C|$.

practice.q: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A=64^\circ$ and $\angle B=76^\circ$. Let $BE$ and $CF$ be altitudes and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Find $\angle EMF$.
practice.hint: Where is the centre of the circle through $B$, $C$, $E$, $F$?
practice.sol:
Here $\angle C=40^\circ$, so the triangle is acute and $E$, $F$ lie on the sides. The right angles $\angle BEC=\angle BFC=90^\circ$ put $E$ and $F$ on the circle with diameter $BC$, whose centre is $M$. So $MB=MC=ME=MF$.

Triangle $MEC$ is isosceles, so $\angle MEC=\angle MCE=40^\circ$ and $\angle EMC=100^\circ$. Triangle $MFB$ is isosceles, so $\angle MFB=\angle MBF=76^\circ$ and $\angle BMF=28^\circ$. These two angles sit on either side of $\angle EMF$ along the line $BC$, so $\angle EMF=180^\circ-100^\circ-28^\circ=52^\circ$. Equivalently, the angle at the centre is twice $\angle ECF=90^\circ-\angle A=26^\circ$.

practice.q: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AB=AD$, and let its diagonals meet at $E$. Prove that $AB$ is tangent to the circle through $B$, $C$ and $E$.
practice.hint: Use the converse of the alternate segment theorem: compare the angle between $AB$ and $BE$ with $\angle BCE$.
practice.sol:
Since $ABCD$ is a convex cyclic quadrilateral, the diagonal $BD$ separates $A$ from $C$, and $E$ lies on both diagonals. Because $AB=AD$, triangle $ABD$ is isosceles and $\angle ABD=\angle ADB$. Angles subtending the same arc $AB$ are equal, so $\angle ADB=\angle ACB$.

Hence $\angle ABE=\angle ABD=\angle ADB=\angle ACB=\angle ECB$, using that $E$ lies on segments $BD$ and $AC$. So the angle between line $AB$ and the chord $BE$ of circle $BCE$ equals the angle $\angle BCE$ subtended by $BE$ at $C$, and $A$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $BE$. By the converse of the alternate segment theorem, $AB$ is tangent to circle $BCE$ at $B$. (With directed angles: $\measuredangle(BA,BE)=\measuredangle ABD=\measuredangle BDA=\measuredangle BCA=\measuredangle BCE$, which is the tangent criterion.)

A useful consequence: the power of $A$ gives $AB^2=AE\cdot AC$.

practice.q: In triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $A$ meets the circumcircle again at $M$, and $I$ is the incentre. Given that $BC=24$, $MI=13$ and $I$ is the midpoint of $AM$, find the circumradius and the perimeter of $ABC$.
practice.hint: The incentre-excentre lemma tells you $MB$. Then look at the right-angled triangle formed by $M$, the midpoint of $BC$ and $B$.
practice.sol:
By the incentre-excentre lemma, $MB=MC=MI=13$. As $M$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$, the line $OM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BC$; let it meet $BC$ at $N$. Then $BN=12$ and, from the right angle at $N$, $MN=\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$.

The centre $O$ lies on line $MN$ with $OM=R$, so $ON=|R-5|$ and Pythagoras in triangle $OBN$ gives $12^2+(R-5)^2=R^2$, that is $169=10R$, so $R=\tfrac{169}{10}$.

For the perimeter, $AM=2\cdot 13=26$ (which is less than the diameter $33.8$, so such a triangle exists). Ptolemy's theorem in the cyclic quadrilateral $ABMC$ gives $AB\cdot MC+AC\cdot MB=AM\cdot BC$, so $13(AB+AC)=26\cdot 24$ and $AB+AC=48$. The perimeter is $48+24=72$.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocentre $H$. The circle through $B$, $H$, $C$ meets lines $AB$ and $AC$ again at points $D$ and $E$, different from $B$ and $C$. Prove that $H$ is the circumcentre of triangle $ADE$.
practice.hint: Prove $HA=HD$ by showing the base angles of triangle $HAD$ are equal. $D$ may be on either side of $B$, so directed angles are worth it.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, since $D$ may lie on segment $AB$ or beyond $B$ (and similarly for $E$). We show $HA=HD$; the same argument with $B$ and $C$ swapped gives $HA=HE$.

First, triangle $HDA$ is genuine. $D\neq A$, because $A$ is not on circle $BHC$: $A$ and $H$ are on the same side of $BC$ and $\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle A\neq\angle A$ as the triangle is acute. Also $H$ is not on line $AB$, since the triangle is acute.

Using that $A,B,D$ are collinear and then that $B,H,C,D$ are concyclic, $\measuredangle HDA=\measuredangle HDB=\measuredangle HCB$. As $CH\perp AB$, $\measuredangle HCB=\measuredangle(CH,AB)+\measuredangle(AB,BC)=90^\circ+\measuredangle(AB,BC)$. On the other hand, as $AH\perp BC$, $\measuredangle DAH=\measuredangle(AB,AH)=\measuredangle(AB,BC)+\measuredangle(BC,AH)=\measuredangle(AB,BC)+90^\circ$.

So $\measuredangle HDA=\measuredangle DAH$. In the triangle $HDA$ these two directed angles are the angles at $D$ and $A$, both measured in the sense of the triangle's orientation, so they equal the ordinary angles with the same sign. Two angles of a triangle that agree modulo $180^\circ$ are equal, so $\angle HDA=\angle DAH$ and $HA=HD$. Together with $HA=HE$, $H$ is equidistant from $A$, $D$, $E$, so it is the circumcentre of $ADE$.

Compare Example 4, where the circle through $B$, $O$, $C$ produced a triangle with orthocentre $O$.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\omega$ and circumcentre $O$. The tangents to $\omega$ at $B$ and $C$ meet at $T$. The line through $T$ parallel to $AB$ meets line $AC$ at $P$. Prove that $PA=PB$.
practice.hint: First show that $P$ lies on the circle through $T$, $B$, $C$. Which other notable point lies on that circle, and what does that say about the angle at $P$?
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. If $CA=CB$ then the tangent at $C$ is parallel to $AB$, so $P=C$ and there is nothing to prove; assume $CA\neq CB$, so $P\neq C$. Also $P\neq T$, since $T$ is not on line $AC$ (otherwise $AC$ would be the tangent at $C$).

Step 1: $T,P,B,C$ are concyclic. As $PT\parallel AB$ and $P$ lies on line $AC$, $\measuredangle TPC=\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle BAC$. By the tangent criterion for the tangent $TB$, $\measuredangle TBC=\measuredangle(BT,BC)=\measuredangle BAC$. Hence $\measuredangle TPC=\measuredangle TBC$, and $T,P,B,C$ are concyclic.

Step 2: $O$ lies on this circle too. The radii $OB$, $OC$ are perpendicular to the tangents, so $\angle OBT=\angle OCT=90^\circ$ and $B$, $C$ lie on the circle with diameter $OT$. That circle is the circle $TBC$, so $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $OT$. If $P=O$ then $PA=PB$ trivially. Otherwise $\angle OPT=90^\circ$.

Step 3. So $OP\perp PT$, and $PT\parallel AB$, hence $OP\perp AB$. The line through $O$ perpendicular to $AB$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, so $P$ lies on it and $PA=PB$. $\blacksquare$

The same argument shows that $P$ lies on circle $BOC$, which links this problem to Example 4.

ladder.note: Two right angles on a common segment give a circle; then bring in the tangent.
Alternate segment theorem, then an exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral.
Show that two angles at L add up to 180 degrees, reading each off a circle.
Pure chasing stalls; an auxiliary point creating an isosceles or equilateral triangle unlocks it.
Draw the common tangent at the point of contact and chase through it.
Isosceles triangles at B plus inscribed angles; directed angles avoid case splits.
Arc midpoints give equal angles; look for a cyclic quadrilateral through P and Q.
Many right angles mean many circles; prove collinearity by angles.
Bring in the centre of the circle and find a circle through P and the tangency points.
Guess the fixed point from a special position of P; arc midpoints are centres of circles through incentres.
Reflections make B equidistant from three points; check whether Q lies on a line through B.
